The world

AdExchanger · 16 Sep 2026

Google's ad tech remedies are public, and the sentence is six years long

Judge Leonie Brinkema's full 106-page remedies opinion in the Google ad tech antitrust case was unsealed on 16 September 2026, two weeks after the ruling itself. She rejected the Department of Justice's request to break up Google's ad tech business, calling structural remedies "neither realistic nor needed." Instead Google must build API integrations linking AdX and DFP to the open-source header-bidding framework Prebid, submit AdX bids to rival publisher ad servers on the same terms DFP gets, and let publishers export their own data. It has 12 months to open AdX to rivals and 12 to 15 months for the Prebid integrations. A court-appointed technical monitor gets full access to Google's employees, systems and source code for six years, the DOJ had asked for fifteen. Final judgment paperwork is due 2 October, and Google is expected to appeal as soon as the order takes effect.

Why it matters "No breakup" was the headline the market wanted, but six years of a monitor with source code access is not nothing. Whether it changes how ad auctions actually run depends entirely on enforcement nobody outside the monitor's office will see, which is exactly the shape of the historical case below.
Digiday, MediaPost · 15 Sep 2026

Google builds the industry's first standard meter for "too many ads"

Google added four new ad metrics, Ad Count, Ad Density, Ad Weight by network use and Ad Weight by CPU use, to its Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX), the same public dataset the industry already uses for Core Web Vitals. Chrome samples the visible viewport once a second for count and density and tracks CPU and network load across the whole session, reporting results at the 75th percentile. Bill Reardon of Google Ads: "Display & Video 360 supports this initiative to bring transparency to page layout quality." No thresholds exist yet, the metrics are still experimental.

Why it matters This is the same week a federal judge forced Google to open its ad exchange to outside data. Here Google is opening data about ad load on its own initiative, with the browser as the instrument. Whether that is a genuine transparency push or a preemptive one is worth asking about every Google announcement this particular week.
Digiday, Editor & Publisher · 15 to 16 Sep 2026

Google will pay publishers when it decides their work "mattered" to an AI answer, and won't say how it decides

Google is quietly scaling a Search Console-based "AI contribution pilot" that pays publishers when it judges their content contributed significantly to a Gemini, AI Overviews or AI Mode response. Publishers who join get an earnings widget showing a monthly number and some history, nothing else: no explanation of how the value is calculated. Reporting on the program describes payouts so far as "peanuts" relative to what the same traffic would have been worth as a click. The rollout follows Judge Amit Mehta's ruling, flagged in a previous issue of this brief, that Google's separate deal with publisher Penske Media over AI Overviews was "deeply unfair."

Why it matters Google is now the judge, the ledger and the only witness in its own AI payments system to the publishers whose traffic it is simultaneously compressing.
MediaPost, Social Media Today · 8 Sep 2026

Reddit opens its AI ad automation to every advertiser

Reddit expanded Max Campaigns, its AI tool that automates targeting, creative, placement and budget, from a limited rollout to all advertisers, and connected it to Reddit's ad API so third-party platforms can manage it. Smartly is the first outside tool plugged in. A new "asset group" feature lets one campaign hold separate creative sets per product line. Reddit's own reported numbers: advertisers on Max Campaigns see 17% lower costs and 27% more conversions than standard campaigns, an internal comparison, not an audited study.

Why it matters Every major ad platform is racing toward the same end state, an AI system that runs the campaign and a human who approves the budget. Reddit just became the latest, not the first.
Digiday, Modern Retail · 15 Sep 2026

Kroger's ad business has its best quarter since 2021

Profit at Kroger Precision Marketing grew 24% in the second quarter, its strongest retail media profit growth since 2021, CEO Greg Foran told investors. Media monetization rose 88 basis points over the past year and e-commerce sales grew 20%, the second straight profitable e-commerce quarter. Foran: "Stronger collaboration between our merchandising and media teams expanded advertising inventory, and optimization efforts improved visibility and conversion for our brand partners." He raised retail media before mentioning traditional merchandising on the earnings call.

Why it matters A grocery chain's ad network outgrowing its core business is no longer an Amazon-only story, and it lands in the same week as three separate Google stories about data, trust and who gets to see it.

Social trends

TikTok · culture-wide · Aug to Sep 2026

Bedazzling everything

  • Started with Kylie Jenner topping her 29th birthday cake with rhinestones in early August; within weeks everything from sheet masks to matcha cups to manicures was getting the treatment.
  • TikTok Insights data cited by Fortune: bedazzling generated 1.08 million searches globally over six months, up 729%, over-indexing with women 18 to 24.
  • It is a screen-off activity, rhinestone kits cost a few dollars, that still produces screen-on content.
Status Hot and still climbing, not yet saturated.
Instagram Reels · Sep 2026

"Corporate Girl"

  • Original sound built around "any girl in the corporate world who gets too many calls in her day," used over clips of packing or unpacking a work bag.
  • Newengen/SocialPilot tracking flags it as a creator-friendly original audio, brand-adaptable by swapping in "___ girl" and a product being packed.
Status Early, climbing.
Instagram Reels · Sep 2026

"10/10 Habits"

  • Rating-hook format: creators share one habit, tip or belief and score it against a literal 10, replacing a vague claim with a specific, checkable number.
  • Lands on the same principle as "Corporate Girl", see Content below.
Status Early per Newengen's September tracking.

Campaigns & brand moves

Media Key · Sep 2026

Deichmann turns "Made in" into "Made for"

Deichmann's "Made for Italy" campaign runs 14 September to 22 November across point of sale, TV, connected TV, online video, CRM, social and the brand's own store, its first campaign built specifically for the Italian market rather than adapted from a pan-European one. The wordplay flips the usual "Made in Italy" prestige claim: the shoes are not defined by where they are made, but by who they are made for. Creative centers the autumn/winter line, pumps, loafers, western and shark boots, styled into an everyday Italian context rather than a runway one.

Why it matters "Accessible, not exclusive" is a hard positioning to hold against actual luxury competitors, but building the entire campaign around a one-word flip of the country's most loaded marketing phrase is a genuinely sharp way to say it without saying it.
Engage, BeautyBiz · 8 to 10 Sep 2026

Armani Beauty builds one fragrance, three local faces

Giorgio Armani's new men's fragrance I Will launched globally with director Todd Field's campaign film fronted by Jonathan Bailey, premiered at the Venice Film Festival. But each major market gets its own "Local Ambassador" layered on top: J Balvin fronts the US, Carlos Sainz fronts Spain, and Luca Argentero now fronts Italy, starring in a dedicated social campaign that runs alongside the global film rather than replacing it.

Why it matters The mechanism is not localization as translation, it is localization as trust. The global campaign buys the reach, and one culturally specific face per market buys the credibility that reach alone cannot.
LBBOnline, Campaign Canada, Publicis Canada · Sep 2026

Rogers turns its own audience into the ad, again

For the third year as TIFF's presenting partner, Rogers and Publicis Canada released "Everyone's a Critic: The Sequel," a follow-up to 2024's original, starring real Torontonians giving unfiltered verdicts on festival films across the 11-day festival. The campaign leans on the fact that TIFF audiences already decide its biggest prize, the People's Choice Award, by vote, so the ads just point a camera at what the festival already does.

Why it matters The mechanism is not casting real people to look authentic, it is that the audience's opinion is structurally the product. The ad campaign and the awards show are describing the same thing from two angles.

What is working in content

Fortune, TikTok Insights · Aug to Sep 2026

Off-screen activities are becoming the content, not just its subject

Bedazzling's appeal, per Fortune's reporting, is partly that it is "an activity that can be done away from a phone," crafting, customizing, personalizing something already owned. The resulting content is not staged, it is a byproduct of someone doing something with their hands, then filming the result.

Why it matters This is the same authenticity premium this brief has tracked all month, just with a physical object standing in for the honest founder video. Content that starts as a real activity is getting rewarded over content built to look like one.
Instagram trend data · Sep 2026

The "specificity beats vagueness" thread keeps confirming itself

A thread flagged in the last issue of this brief, that specific, checkable claims beat vague self-improvement talk, shows up again this week. "10/10 Habits" replaces "this changed my life" with an actual score. "Corporate Girl" replaces "I'm so busy" with the literal contents of a bag. Neither trend needed a celebrity or a studio budget, both needed one real, nameable detail.

Why it matters Three issues in a row have surfaced the same principle from unrelated sources without citing each other. At this point it is less a trend and more a rule: if a hook cannot be fact-checked in one second, it is losing to one that can.

The historical bridge

Washington DC, 2000 to 2002

Microsoft avoided a breakup too, and the oversight ran nine years instead of five

In June 2000, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson found Microsoft had illegally maintained its Windows monopoly and ordered the company split into two, an operating systems company and an applications company. Microsoft appealed. In June 2001, the DC Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously overturned the breakup order, kept the underlying monopoly finding, and removed Jackson from the case entirely for talking to reporters about the trial. Weeks later the Department of Justice announced it would no longer pursue a breakup. What replaced it, finalized as a consent decree in November 2002 under Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly, was a five-year settlement requiring Microsoft to disclose its Windows APIs to outside developers, license software to computer makers on uniform, non-exclusionary terms, and submit to an independent three-person Technical Committee empowered to field complaints and inspect Microsoft's systems. The decree was extended twice. It did not fully expire until May 2011, nine years after it was signed, more than a decade after the original ruling.

Why it still holds. Google's ad tech remedies follow the exact same arc. DOJ sought a breakup, a judge called it unnecessary, and what took its place is a fixed-term technical monitor with deep access, negotiated down from what the government wanted: fifteen years asked for, six years given, much like Microsoft's Technical Committee, five years asked, nine years actually served. Nobody in 2002 could have said in month one whether Microsoft's decree would actually change the market or just generate compliance paperwork, it took most of the decade to find out. Google's monitor has its first real deadlines in 12 to 15 months. The honest answer to whether this remedy works is not available yet, and won't be for years, exactly as it wasn't for Microsoft.
